description_full: FS Bancorp, Inc. operates as a bank holding company for 1st Security Bank of Washington that provides banking and financial services to local families, local and regional businesses, and industry niches in Washington. The company operates in two segments, Commercial and Consumer Banking; and Home Lending. It offers various deposit instruments, including checking accounts, money market deposit accounts, savings accounts, and certificates of deposit. The company provides one-to-four-family residential first mortgages loans, home equity loan products, commercial business loans, commercial real estate loans, and construction and development loans, as well as consumer loans, which include personal lines of credit, credit cards, automobile, direct home improvement, loans on deposit, and recreational loans. Further, it provides online banking platforms, mobile banking apps, and telephone banking services, as well as cash management services. The company operates full bank service branches and home loan production offices in suburban communities in the greater Puget Sound area, including Snohomish, King, Pierce, Kitsap, Clallam, Jefferson, Grays Harbor, Thurston, and Benton counties; Oregon; and a loan production office in the market area of the Tri-Cities. The company was founded in 1936 and is headquartered in Mountlake Terrace, Washington.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 626 people. Revenue per employee of $244K ranks in the bottom quartile among Financial Services peers, improving at 16%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $83K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: FS Bancorp, Inc. is a small-cap financial services business with a $343M market cap on $153M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 8% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $52M in free cash flow — roughly 34 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.17× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 7.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 8.4% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.3) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: Trading at a 47% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
12 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 27% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.04x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-13.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 18% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.66, it is more defensive than the market.
About $1.1M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.7x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 53% in the 2020 crash and 22% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 47% below its DCF fair value of $82.13, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 20%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $62.94 to $112 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 6.6 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 25% above its 10-year median.
The 2 covering analysts target $45.50 on average, 4% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 13.9% annual cash-flow growth, 12pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.1%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.31).
It converts 34% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 11% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.7% over 3 years, 3.4% over 5 years and 12.8% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 53% of profits supports about 6.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
It has missed earnings estimates by 18.6% on average.
Analysts expect 13.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 8.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 67%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $435K sold).
It returns 7.5% a year to shareholders (4.5% in buybacks and 2.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 23.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 626 employees, each generates about $244K of revenue, 0.5x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 15.8% a year.
That works out to $83K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $728K (3x revenue per employee).
